title: Where Global Tech Hiring Is Shifting
summary: The question is not which region wins the technology race. It is how employers convert demand for a specialized skill into a vacancy that a candidate can actually accept. Location rules, pay transparency, employer scale and infrastructure shape that conversion.

blocks.text: U.S. job access, European skills demand and the African employment conversion challenge
The U.S. baseline is broader than tech

September 2026 U.S. job openings were about 7.5 million across the entire economy, not seven and a half million technology vacancies. For specialists in business intelligence, data engineering and healthcare analytics, a useful measure must isolate postings by occupation, skill, industry and permitted work location. A national headline alone cannot answer whether a remote applicant has strong prospects.
Europe has skills demand and national boundaries

Eurostat recorded about 10.45 million employed ICT specialists in the EU in 2025. Germany’s IT vacancy estimates declined from 149,000 in 2023 to around 79,000 in 2026, illustrating why talent shortages and softening demand can coexist. The five-country sample includes the United Kingdom, Germany, France, the Netherlands and Spain. Remote within one country is not equivalent to worldwide remote or visa sponsorship.
Africa: talent capacity versus formal placement

The World Bank estimates that millions of young people enter the labor market each year in Eastern and Southern Africa while far fewer obtain wage employment. That estimate is not specific to technology occupations. Within the reviewed tech vacancy sample, demand appears in South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana and Egypt, but the sample cannot quantify the continent’s total demand. Measure the journey from training to interviews, offers, wages and retention instead.

Build a standardized vacancy sample for each region: unique verified postings, age of posting, skills requested, published salary, country eligibility, work authorization and final application status. Only then can we compare the share of internationally accessible technical opportunities and identify changes that are larger than sampling noise.
